entries.seminar_title: The Volatility of Marginal Information Rents in Dynamic Mechanism Design
entries.speaker: Daniel Chen
entries.abstract: This paper brings martingale methods of continuous-time contracting to Myersonian dynamic mechanism design. In a benchmark setting, I show that implementability is characterized by the volatility of the agent's marginal information rent—how the marginal rent responds to innovations in his type. Once transfers satisfy the usual envelope conditions, truthful reporting after the initial report is locally incentive compatible if and only if the discounted volatility is a nonnegative supermartingale. When the volatility has finite variation, the same condition is necessary and sufficient for global incentive compatibility after the initial report. Using this characterization, I cast the design problem as optimal control, which applies even when the first-order approach fails: one program solves for the optimal mechanism in a regular finite-variation class, and another for the optimal locally incentive-compatible mechanism. The two bracket the designer's true payoff. I apply the results to financial market design (a monopolistic dealer, then an exchange).
entries.bio:
Daniel Chen
Assistant Professor of Economics
Princeton University

entries.speaker: Sean Reese
entries.abstract: Accelerating biodiversity loss has intensified the pressure on firms to offset their ecological impacts. We present the first comprehensive evaluation of one of the world's oldest biodiversity offset policies: compensatory mitigation under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. By combining four decades of satellite land-use imagery with ecological survey and citizen science data, we find that highly regulated offset projects (“conservation banks”) yield positive ecological spillovers and curb internal land-use pressure, but less supervised offsetting projects ("permittee-responsible mitigation") do not. Despite these localized gains, conservation banks are poorly sited across space. Using a stylized model of optimal bank placement, we demonstrate that conservation banks are systematically located in areas with minimal threats of development, calling into question their additionality. This inefficiency stems from a core policy design flaw: offset creation operates strictly on the extensive margin, generating offsets based on land area while failing to discriminate based on threat level or habitat quality. As voluntary and regulatory biodiversity markets expand worldwide, these results emphasize that offset frameworks must incorporate conversion risk to ensure additionality.
entries.bio:
Sean Reese
PhD Student in Sustainable Development
Columbia University

entries.seminar_title: Pricing wildfire smoke avoidance: activity reallocation from mobility data
entries.speaker: Clara Berestycki
entries.abstract: This paper estimates the welfare cost of avoiding wildfire smoke during the 2018 Northern California fire season. Using individual smartphone location data, I construct daily ZIP-to-ZIP trip flows across activity types, including outdoor recreation, work, and other trips. I embed these flows in a nested logit model of activity participation and destination choice, with destination choice estimated as a gravity equation over a comprehensive choice set. Smoke deters both leaving home and visiting polluted locations. I find that people substitute away from smoky outdoor destinations, and that wildfire smoke shifts the composition of daily activities: the share of outdoor activities falls, but so do the shares of work and other trips. The welfare cost of this avoidance behavior is around $500M, adding 14% to the mortality burden of the same smoke. Air quality alerts increase avoidance, and under alert-level awareness of moderate smoke, welfare costs would be 20% higher.
entries.bio:
Clara Berestycki
PhD Student in Sustainable Development
Columbia University
